doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

chapter: The music industry and the press
title: Critics and music journalism
summary: Journalism has become hype, and writers misread musicians' intentions.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Sometimes I think people create one so they have something to write about.

I think so. And honestly I think writers tend to write for each other. And I have seen some articles, as a matter of fact I have sort of taken a moratorium against some of the publications because I think — even some of the more popular music publications — because I have copies of articles from the 1960s and 70s, where the journalism is really getting into what it is about the musician, and what the musician is thinking about and what the musician is doing. Now it’s, in the last ten years, it’s become this hype machine. And it’s really not about, at least always, it’s not about the musician. It’s about some other factor in the industry. And I’ve even read articles, I’ve even read reviews of my own records where writers are saying something, even when they’re trying to say something positive, they’re totally off base as to what I’m trying to do musically. And I look at it and go oh is that what I was thinking about. Oh I’m glad he knows. Because I wasn’t thinking about anything when I wrote that. So I really do think that there are writers out there who are responsible. I think there are responsible journalists. But we now have more than our share of those who don’t know the music, they don’t understand what it is to be an artist, so they can’t speak from that perspective, so what right do they © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
have to judge what artists are trying to do? So yeah, I think there’s a negative effect out there right now.
